ai_summary: Great Britain is currently generating 11.1 GW of wind power, with estimated Scottish wind output standing at 4.3 GW, which represents 42.6% of installed Scottish wind capacity. This robust renewable output maintains Scottish carbon intensity at an immaculate 0 gCO2/kWh, in sharp contrast to 59 gCO2/kWh GB-wide. However, persistent cross-border transmission bottlenecks prevent this surplus green energy from flowing freely southward. Consequently, Scottish generation curtailed so far today has reached 17.8 GWh through Balancing Mechanism bids, racking up a constraint cost of about £1,009,064. To make up for this stranded zero-carbon power, thermal plants had to be dispatched downstream, requiring an estimated 3,387,738 m3 of gas burned elsewhere and generating 6,241 tonnes of avoidable CO2 emissions. Annualising today's expenditure highlights the heavy financial burden of these grid bottlenecks, yielding an estimated total yearly cost of curtailment of £368 million. Distributed across national demand, this operational constraint increases everybody's invoice in the UK by an estimated £1/MWh, illustrating how transmission network limitations simultaneously drive up retail power bills and diminish decarbonisation gains.
